assessment.name: Year 8 Music Autumn assessment
assessment.sections: Assessed in class during the assessment window (30 November to 9 December). Autumn unit: djembe drumming and singing. Expect a performance plus questions on the key words.
assessment.weighting: Built from the Ark curriculum unit only (no school revision list yet): djembe sounds and technique, African drumming features, rhythm and notation, and singing skills.

mock.note: 20 questions on djembe, African drumming and musical key words. Practise your rhythm out loud too.

units.name: Rhythm, notation and the musical elements

cards.title: The djembe
cards.question: What is a djembe, and where does it come from?
points: The djembe is a goblet shaped drum from West Africa, especially Mali and Guinea.
It is traditionally carved from one piece of wood, with a goat skin head tightened by ropes.
It is played with bare hands, not sticks.
Djembes are often played with deeper bass drums called dunun (or dundun), which are played with sticks.
cards.watch_out: The djembe is a hand drum. The dunun are the drums played with sticks.
cards.hook: Djembe: goblet shape, goat skin, bare hands.
cards.grade9: Explain the role of drumming in West African life: it is used for celebrations, ceremonies, work and storytelling.

cards.title: The three djembe sounds
cards.question: How do you play the bass, tone and slap sounds?
points: Bass: hit the centre of the drum with a flat palm. Low, deep sound.
Tone: hit near the edge with your fingers together and flat. Clear, medium pitched sound.
Slap: hit near the edge with relaxed, slightly spread fingers that whip the skin. High, sharp sound.
Let your hand bounce off the skin so the drum can ring.
cards.watch_out: Tone and slap are both played near the edge. The difference is the hand: fingers together for tone, relaxed and loose for slap.
cards.hook: Bass in the middle, tone and slap at the edge.
cards.grade9: Control the three sounds so each is clearly different, even at a fast tempo.

cards.title: Playing technique and posture
cards.question: How should you sit and play the djembe?
points: Sit on the front of the chair with the drum between your knees, tilted slightly away from you so the sound can escape underneath.
Keep your back straight and shoulders relaxed.
Use your arms and wrists, not just your fingers, and let your hands bounce off.
Alternate hands (right, left) to keep rhythms smooth.
cards.watch_out: If the drum is flat on the floor, the sound is muffled. Tilt it.
cards.grade9: Play rhythms with a steady, even sound in both hands so neither hand is louder.

cards.title: Call and response
cards.question: What is call and response in African drumming?
points: A leader plays or sings a phrase (the call).
The group answers with a reply (the response).
The master drummer uses a signal (or break) to start, stop or change the rhythm.
It keeps the whole group together and lets the leader direct the performance.
cards.watch_out: Watch and listen to the leader. Coming in late after the call is the most common mistake.
cards.grade9: Explain why call and response suits an oral tradition: everyone learns by listening and copying, not by reading music.

cards.title: Polyrhythm, ostinato and cyclic rhythm
cards.question: What are polyrhythm, ostinato and cyclic rhythm?
points: Ostinato: a short rhythm or pattern that repeats over and over.
Cyclic rhythm: rhythms that repeat in a cycle, often for a long time.
Polyrhythm: several different rhythms played at the same time, which fit together.
Each player must keep their own part steady while others play different patterns.
cards.watch_out: Polyrhythm means many rhythms at once, not one complicated rhythm.
cards.hook: Poly = many (polygon has many sides), so polyrhythm = many rhythms.
cards.grade9: Hold your ostinato steady while listening to how it fits with the other parts in the polyrhythm.

cards.title: Master drummer, improvisation and oral tradition
cards.question: What is the role of the master drummer, and how is the music passed on?
points: The master drummer leads the group, plays signals and often improvises solos.
Improvisation means making up music on the spot.
Oral tradition: the music is learned by ear and passed from person to person, not written down.
Players often learn rhythms using spoken sounds or words to remember them.
cards.watch_out: Improvisation is planned within the style and pulse; it is not random noise.
cards.grade9: Improvise a short solo over the group's ostinato that still keeps to the pulse.

cards.title: Pulse, rhythm and tempo
cards.question: What is the difference between pulse, rhythm and tempo?
points: Pulse (or beat): the steady beat underneath the music, like a heartbeat.
Rhythm: the pattern of long and short sounds played over the pulse.
Tempo: the speed of the pulse. Accelerando means getting faster; rallentando means getting slower.
Unison: everyone playing the same rhythm at the same time.
cards.watch_out: Pulse stays steady; rhythm changes. Rushing (speeding up by accident) is a common problem in groups.
cards.hook: Pulse is the heartbeat; rhythm is the dance on top.
cards.grade9: Keep the pulse in your head or by tapping your foot while playing a complicated rhythm.

cards.title: Rhythm notation
cards.question: How long do the main notes and rests last?
points: Semibreve: 4 beats. Minim: 2 beats. Crotchet: 1 beat. Quaver: half a beat (two quavers make one beat).
Semiquaver: a quarter of a beat (four make one beat).
A rest is a silence that lasts the same length as its note.
In 4/4 time there are four crotchet beats in each bar.
cards.watch_out: A quaver is half a beat, not a quarter. Four semiquavers make one crotchet.
cards.grade9: Write a 4 beat djembe rhythm in notation, using B, T and S above the notes for bass, tone and slap.

cards.title: Dynamics and the other elements
cards.question: Which musical elements should you use to describe a performance?
points: Dynamics: how loud or quiet. Piano (p) quiet, forte (f) loud, crescendo getting louder, diminuendo getting quieter.
Pitch: how high or low. Bass is low pitched; slap is high pitched.
Texture: how many layers of sound. Polyrhythm creates a thick texture.
Timbre: the type or quality of sound, such as the sharp slap or deep bass.
Structure: how the piece is organised, such as call and response or verse and chorus.
cards.watch_out: Use the Italian words (piano, forte) correctly: piano here means quiet, not the instrument.
cards.hook: Dynamics are about decibels: loud and soft.
cards.grade9: Describe a performance using at least four elements, such as tempo, dynamics, texture and timbre.

cards.title: Singing skills
cards.question: How do you sing well in a group?
points: Posture: stand tall with feet apart, shoulders relaxed and head up.
Breathing: breathe low into your stomach (diaphragm), not your shoulders, and take breaths at the ends of phrases.
Warm up your voice with humming, sirens and tongue twisters before singing.
Diction: say the words clearly. Pitch: sing in tune by listening to others and the accompaniment.
cards.watch_out: Breathing in the middle of a word breaks the phrase. Plan where to breathe.
cards.grade9: Sing a harmony part or a round (canon) while staying in tune with your own part.

cards.title: Performing in a group
cards.question: What do teachers look for in a group performance assessment?
points: Accuracy: the right rhythms, sounds and words.
Timing: keeping in time with the pulse and the group.
Ensemble: listening, watching the leader, starting and stopping together.
Expression and confidence: using dynamics and performing with energy.
cards.watch_out: If you make a mistake, keep going and rejoin at the next bar. Stopping affects the whole group.
cards.grade9: Lead a call or a section confidently, or add a planned dynamic change that the group follows.

cards.title: Key words checklist
cards.question: Can you define each music key word?
points: Djembe, dunun, bass, tone, slap.
Call and response, signal, master drummer, improvisation, oral tradition.
Ostinato, cyclic rhythm, polyrhythm, unison.
Pulse, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, pitch, texture, timbre, structure.
Posture, breathing, diction, warm up, harmony.
cards.watch_out: Learn one example for each word from your djembe or singing lessons.

written.q: Describe how to play the three main sounds on the djembe.
model: Bass: flat palm in the centre, low sound (1)
Tone: fingers together near the edge, clear medium sound (1)
Slap: relaxed fingers near the edge, high sharp sound (1)

written.q: Describe three features of West African drumming music.
model: Call and response between a leader and the group (1)
Polyrhythm: different rhythms played at the same time (1)
Ostinato or cyclic rhythms that repeat (1)
Improvisation by the master drummer, or oral tradition (1)

written.q: Give four tips for a successful group singing performance.
model: Good posture: stand tall, shoulders relaxed (1)
Breathe from the diaphragm at the ends of phrases (1)
Listen to stay in tune and in time with the group (1)

exam_tips.timing: The performance is assessed in class. Practise your part every day this week, even by tapping on a table.
section_a: Learn the key words and their meanings.
Know the three djembe sounds and how to play each.
section_b: Keep in time with the pulse and watch the leader.
Use dynamics to make your performance expressive.
If you slip, keep going and rejoin.
